title: Classic ASP.NET error page disclosed in a response
description: The response carries the fixed heading of the classic ASP.NET unhandled-exception page. That page prints the exception message, the source line and a stack frame naming the assembly, and it is emitted by default outside a custom-errors configuration.
remediation: Set <customErrors mode="On" /> (or On with a defaultRedirect) in Web.config and return a generic page with a correlation id.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the page heading; it does not decide whether the stack below it names internal paths.
scopeT: One response body containing the classic ASP.NET error heading.
fp: A documentation page that quotes the heading is reported; an ASP.NET Core developer page is handled by DPK-DAST-127 instead and does not contain this heading.
recordDesc: The classic ASP.NET unhandled-exception page prints the exception message, the failing source line and an assembly-qualified stack frame. Serving it discloses the application layout and the exact line that failed, which is the reconnaissance a targeted exploit needs.
applicability: Responses generated by an ASP.NET application running with custom errors disabled.
risk: The caller reads the exception message and the assembly and source paths of the failing handler, which describes the application internals and the code path to attack next.
why: The body contains the classic ASP.NET unrecoverable-error heading.
fix: Enable customErrors in Web.config and redirect to a static page.
Log the exception server-side with a correlation id.
verifyT: Raise an unhandled exception with custom errors on and confirm the response carries no heading, message or stack.

observation.body: Description: An unhandled exception occurred.
An unhandled exception occurred while processing the request. Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.DeveloperExceptionPageMiddleware

title: ASP.NET trace application disclosed in a response
description: The response is the ASP.NET trace viewer: it names trace.axd and the Application Trace table. The viewer lists every recent request with its headers, session identifiers and form values, so an exposed instance discloses other users' data as well as the application internals.
remediation: Disable tracing in production (<trace enabled="false" />) and block trace.axd at the web server. Treat every recorded request as disclosed.
limitation: One response body. The check recognises the trace viewer; it does not enumerate the recorded requests.
scopeT: One response body containing both the trace.axd reference and the Application Trace table.
fp: A page that merely links to trace.axd is reported only when the Application Trace table is also present; a tutorial page discussing ASP.NET tracing is not.
recordDesc: The ASP.NET trace viewer lists recent requests with their headers, session identifiers, form and query values. When it is reachable it discloses other users' request data, not just the application layout, and the session identifiers alone are enough to hijack a live session.
applicability: Responses served by an ASP.NET application with tracing enabled.
risk: The caller reads other users' session identifiers, form values and request headers, which enables session hijacking and discloses the application's internal request shapes.
why: The body contains the ASP.NET trace viewer with its request table.
fix: Disable tracing in production configuration.
Block trace.axd at the web server and review the recorded requests as disclosed.
verifyT: Request trace.axd on a production deployment and confirm the server answers 404 rather than a request table.

title: Node.js inspector debugging endpoint disclosed
description: The response is the Node.js inspector target list: a JSON or HTML page carrying a webSocketDebuggerUrl. Anyone who can reach that URL attaches a debugger to the live process, reads memory and executes code in it, so this is not an information leak but remote code execution waiting to be used.
remediation: Never bind the inspector to a public interface: start node with --inspect=127.0.0.1 (or omit it in production) and block the inspector port at the network boundary.
limitation: One response body. The check proves the endpoint answered; it does not attach to the debugger or prove that the socket is still open.
scopeT: One response body containing the inspector target list with a webSocketDebuggerUrl field.
fp: A documentation page that quotes the field name is reported; an application that merely mentions --inspect in a help page is not unless the field name is present.
recordDesc: The Node.js inspector publishes a target list containing webSocketDebuggerUrl. That URL accepts a debugger session on the live process, which reads and writes memory and evaluates arbitrary code with the service account's privileges. Exposure is equivalent to remote code execution.
applicability: Responses served by a Node.js process started with the inspector enabled on a reachable interface.
risk: The caller attaches a debugger to the production process, reads secrets from memory and executes arbitrary code in the service context.
why: The body contains an inspector target list with a debugger socket URL.
fix: Start the process with --inspect bound to 127.0.0.1 or not at all.
Block the inspector port and rotate every secret the process could read.
verifyT: Request the inspector path from outside the host and confirm the connection is refused.

observation.body: Start the service with --inspect and attach your editor.

title: Served source map embeds the original source code
description: The response is a source map whose sourcesContent field carries the original files. A map with only file names helps debugging; a map with sourcesContent publishes the pre-build source to anyone who opens the developer tools, including comments and internal URLs.
remediation: Build production maps without sourcesContent, serve maps only to authenticated users, or omit the maps from the public build.
limitation: One response body. The check proves the source text is embedded; it does not read the application code or decide whether that code is sensitive.
scopeT: One response body containing a source map with a sourcesContent array.
fp: A map that lists sources without sourcesContent is not reported; a page that discusses source maps in prose is not reported unless the field name appears as JSON.
recordDesc: A source map with sourcesContent embeds the original files, comments and internal URLs next to the minified build. Serving it hands the application source to anyone who opens developer tools, which removes the only real benefit of minifying and often discloses endpoints that never appear in the shipped bundle.
applicability: Responses that serve JavaScript, CSS or any compiled asset together with its source map.
risk: The caller reads the original source, its comments and any internal hosts or feature flags named there, which supports targeted exploitation and endpoint discovery.
why: The body is a source map that embeds the original sources.
fix: Emit production source maps without sourcesContent.
Restrict map access to authenticated users or drop the maps from the public build.
verifyT: Fetch a production map and confirm it lists file names without a sourcesContent array.

observation.body: Set devtool to hidden-source-map to drop the source reference from the bundle.

title: Symfony VarDumper output disclosed in a response
description: The response contains a Symfony VarDumper block. VarDumper prints the full value graph of whatever it is given, including object properties, request attributes and environment values, and it is normally removed before production.
remediation: Remove every dump/dd() call from a production build and disable the debug bundle outside development.
limitation: One response body. The check recognises the dump markup; it does not enumerate which values were printed.
scopeT: One response body containing the VarDumper block markup.
fp: A Symfony documentation page that shows the markup is reported; the profiler toolbar (DPK-DAST-244) and a plain debug print are not, because they carry different markers.
recordDesc: Symfony VarDumper prints the complete value graph of the object it receives, including private properties, request attributes and environment values. A dump left in a production response therefore discloses data the page never intended to render, often including credentials held in configuration objects.
applicability: Responses generated by a Symfony application that still contains a dump or dd() call.
risk: The caller reads configuration values, request attributes and object internals that the endpoint does not otherwise expose, which can include credentials and internal host names.
why: The body contains a Symfony VarDumper block.
fix: Remove dump() and dd() calls from the production build.
Disable the debug bundle outside development.
verifyT: Search a production response for the VarDumper markup and confirm it is absent.

title: Xdebug variable dump disclosed in a response
description: The response carries an Xdebug var_dump() block. Xdebug renders variables as HTML with the file path, line number and the full value tree, so a dump left in production discloses the code location and whatever the variable held.
remediation: Turn Xdebug off in production (xdebug.mode=off) and remove every var_dump()/dump() call from deployed code.
limitation: One response body. The check recognises the dump markup; it does not read the dumped values.
scopeT: One response body containing the Xdebug dump block.
fp: A PHP tutorial that shows the markup is reported; the plain PHP var_dump() output without Xdebug is not matched by this rule and is covered by DPK-DAST-067 when it carries a source path.
recordDesc: Xdebug renders var_dump() as HTML carrying the file path, the line number and the full value tree. A dump left in production discloses the exact code location and the data that reached it, which is both a source map and a data leak in one response.
applicability: Responses generated by a PHP application with Xdebug enabled in a deployed environment.
risk: The caller learns file paths, line numbers and the contents of variables that may hold credentials, tokens or personal data.
why: The body contains the Xdebug dump block.
fix: Set xdebug.mode=off in the production PHP configuration.
Remove var_dump() and dump() calls from deployed code.
verifyT: Request a page that used to dump and confirm no Xdebug markup is present.

observation.body: Warning: Undefined array key "q" in /var/www/search.php on line 12

title: Set-Cookie attribute name is misspelt so the browser ignores it
description: A Set-Cookie value spells a security attribute with a separator or a typo: Http-Only, http_only, Same-Site= or Seccure. Browsers match attribute names exactly, so the intended protection is silently absent while the header looks protected to a reviewer.
remediation: Emit the attribute names exactly as the specification defines them (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite) and add a test that asserts the emitted header string.
limitation: One Set-Cookie value. The check reads the attribute name; it does not decide which protection the author intended.
scopeT: One Set-Cookie value containing a misspelt Secure, HttpOnly or SameSite attribute name.
fp: A correctly spelled Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite attribute is not reported; a cookie value that happens to contain these words after the first semicolon is unlikely but would be reported, which is why the pattern requires the attribute position.
recordDesc: Cookie attribute names are matched exactly, so Http-Only, http_only, Same-Site and Seccure are inert text. The header then looks protected in a code review and in a header dump while the browser enforces nothing, which is worse than an obviously missing attribute because no reviewer looks twice at a header that appears to carry it.
applicability: Responses that set cookies through the header.
risk: The cookie is stored without the protection the author intended: without HttpOnly it is readable from script, without Secure it travels on plaintext requests, and a broken SameSite allows cross-site sends.
why: A Set-Cookie attribute name uses a separator or a spelling a browser does not match.
fix: Emit Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite with exactly these names.
Assert the emitted header string in a test.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm every security attribute name matches the specification spelling.

title: Set-Cookie Domain is a public suffix
description: The Domain attribute names a public suffix such as com, co.uk or github.io. A browser rejects the cookie outright, and a client that accepts it would share the cookie with every site under that suffix, so the configuration either drops the session or leaks it.
remediation: Set Domain to the application host or to a registrable domain the organisation controls, or omit Domain so the cookie stays host-only.
limitation: One Set-Cookie value. The check uses a fixed list of well-known public suffixes; a suffix outside that list is not detected.
scopeT: One Set-Cookie value whose Domain attribute is a public suffix from the built-in list.
fp: A Domain that ends with a listed suffix but has a registrable label before it (example.com) is not reported; a private-company suffix outside the list is not reported and is stated here as a limitation.
recordDesc: A cookie scoped to a public suffix is either rejected by the browser, which loses the session, or accepted by a permissive client, which sends it to every registrant under that suffix. Both outcomes are bad and neither is visible in a header dump that looks correct at a glance.
applicability: Responses that set cookies with an explicit Domain attribute.
risk: The session cookie is dropped in enforcing browsers, or is sent to unrelated sites under the same public suffix, where any registrant can read it.
why: The Domain attribute is a public suffix rather than a host the site controls.
fix: Omit Domain so the cookie is host-only, or name a registrable domain the organisation owns.
Check the emitted header in a browser and in a test.
verifyT: Set the cookie and confirm the browser stores it for the intended host only, not for a public suffix.

title: Set-Cookie Partitioned is sent without Secure
description: A cookie carries the Partitioned attribute but not Secure. The specification requires Secure with Partitioned, so browsers discard the cookie: the partitioned storage the author asked for never exists, and the failure is silent.
remediation: Always pair Partitioned with Secure and SameSite=None; consider the __Host- prefix so the whole contract is enforced by the browser.
limitation: One Set-Cookie value. The check reads the attributes; it does not test which user agents implement partitioned storage.
scopeT: One Set-Cookie value carrying Partitioned without Secure.
fp: A cookie with both Partitioned and Secure is not reported; a cookie using SameSite=None without Partitioned is covered by DPK-DAST-265 instead.
recordDesc: Partitioned cookies are only stored when Secure is also present, so the pair is a contract the browser enforces by discarding the header. Sending Partitioned alone silently loses the cookie, and because the header looks modern in review the defect tends to survive until a user reports being logged out.
applicability: Responses that set cookies with the Partitioned attribute.
risk: The cookie is discarded in enforcing browsers, so embedded or cross-site flows lose their session state without an error anywhere.
why: The Set-Cookie value carries Partitioned without Secure.
fix: Always send Partitioned together with Secure and SameSite=None.
Use the __Host- prefix so the browser enforces path and host scope too.
verifyT: Set the cookie and confirm the browser keeps it for the embedded context.

title: Server header names an internal host
description: The Server header carries a private-suffix hostname such as app.internal, build.local or svc.corp rather than a product token. That names the internal naming scheme and often the environment, which is exactly what an attacker needs to guess the next host to reach.
remediation: Suppress or normalise the Server header at the edge so it carries a product token or nothing, never an internal hostname.
limitation: One Server header value. The check reads the name; it does not resolve it and cannot confirm the host exists.
scopeT: One Server header whose value contains a private-suffix hostname.
fp: A product token such as nginx or cloudflare is not reported, and a version disclosure is covered by DPK-DAST-030 instead.
recordDesc: Internal hostnames follow a house naming scheme and often encode environment, region and role. Publishing one in the Server header tells the caller how the private network is named, which turns a single exposed host into a map of the estate and shortens the search for a second target.
applicability: Responses emitted by an origin or proxy that forwards its own hostname in the Server header.
risk: The caller learns the internal naming scheme and environment, which supports lateral targeting and makes internal-only hosts discoverable by name.
why: The Server header value is an internal hostname rather than a product token.
fix: Normalise or suppress the Server header at the edge.
Keep internal hostnames out of every response header.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint through the public edge and confirm the Server header carries no private-suffix hostname.

title: iframe sandbox combines allow-scripts with allow-same-origin
description: An iframe carries sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin". That pair is documented as equivalent to no sandbox: the framed document runs script in the parent origin, can read the parent DOM and can remove its own sandbox attribute.
remediation: Drop one of the two tokens. Serve untrusted content with allow-scripts only (and a separate origin), or with allow-same-origin only when no script is needed.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the sandbox attribute; it does not execute the frame and cannot see attributes added at runtime.
scopeT: One iframe element whose sandbox attribute carries both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin.
fp: A frame with only allow-scripts or only allow-same-origin is not reported; documentation that quotes the dangerous pair inside a code block is reported, which is stated as a known false positive.
recordDesc: allow-scripts together with allow-same-origin is the documented way to defeat a sandbox: the frame keeps the parent origin and can script it, including removing its own sandbox attribute. Reviewers see two reassuring tokens and the protection is gone, so the pair has to be treated as no sandbox at all.
applicability: Responses that embed an iframe with a sandbox attribute.
risk: Content framed from an untrusted source runs script in the embedding origin, reads the parent DOM and can act with the user's session on that origin.
why: An iframe sandbox carries both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin.
fix: Remove one of the two tokens from the sandbox attribute.
Serve untrusted content from a separate origin with allow-scripts only.
verifyT: Load the page and confirm the framed document cannot reach the parent DOM.

observation.body: <iframe width='600' height='400' src='/preview' sandbox='allow-same-origin allow-scripts allow-forms'></iframe>

title: Meta tag delivers a CSP frame-ancestors directive a browser ignores
description: The page carries a Content-Security-Policy meta tag that declares frame-ancestors. Browsers ignore frame-ancestors when it arrives in a meta element, so the framing restriction the author wrote never applies and the page stays embeddable by any origin.
remediation: Send Content-Security-Policy as a response header; frame-ancestors and report-uri are only honoured there. Keep X-Frame-Options as a second layer.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the meta tag; it cannot see a header that the App header allowlist may have dropped, and it does not test framing behaviour.
scopeT: One meta element whose http-equiv is Content-Security-Policy and whose content carries frame-ancestors.
fp: A meta CSP without frame-ancestors is not reported; a page that documents the restriction in prose is not reported unless the meta element is present.
recordDesc: Several CSP directives, frame-ancestors among them, are ignored when the policy arrives in a meta element, because the browser cannot apply them after the document has started parsing. A team that writes frame-ancestors in a meta tag therefore believes it has blocked framing while every origin can still embed the page.
applicability: Responses that deliver a Content-Security-Policy through a meta element.
risk: The page remains embeddable by any origin, which enables clickjacking and UI redressing against authenticated users despite the declared policy.
why: A meta element declares frame-ancestors inside a CSP that browsers will not enforce in that position.
fix: Send Content-Security-Policy as a response header instead of a meta tag.
Keep X-Frame-Options as a second layer.
verifyT: Load the page in a frame from another origin and confirm the browser blocks it.

title: Meta tag delivers a CSP that permits inline script
description: The page declares its Content-Security-Policy in a meta tag and that policy carries unsafe-inline. The policy can neither stop an injected inline script nor be tightened with hashes later, and because it arrives in the body it is also the easiest policy to remove by an injection.
remediation: Send the policy as a response header and remove unsafe-inline in favour of nonces or hashes.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the meta element; it does not evaluate whether other directives would still block a specific payload.
scopeT: One meta element declaring a CSP whose content carries unsafe-inline.
fp: A meta CSP without unsafe-inline is not reported; a header-delivered policy is covered by the header rules instead.
recordDesc: unsafe-inline removes the main benefit of a script policy, and a policy delivered in a meta element is both weaker and easier to strip during injection. The combination leaves the page looking protected in a source review while inline script executes freely.
applicability: Responses that deliver a Content-Security-Policy through a meta element.
risk: An injected inline script executes in the page origin, which allows session theft and page rewriting despite the declared policy.
why: A meta element declares a CSP that allows inline script.
fix: Send the policy as a response header.
Replace unsafe-inline with a nonce or hash.
verifyT: Inject an inline script in a test build and confirm the browser blocks it.

title: Meta referrer tag sends full URLs to every destination
description: A meta referrer element sets unsafe-url, which sends the complete URL of the page to every destination, including cross-origin and plaintext ones. Query strings that carry tokens, identifiers and invitation keys then travel in the Referer header of every outbound request.
remediation: Remove the meta tag and set Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin as a response header, which is the browser default and cannot be overridden by page content.
limitation: One response body. The check reads the meta element; it does not observe the Referer header the browser later sends.
scopeT: One meta referrer element whose content is unsafe-url.
fp: A meta referrer tag with a stricter policy is not reported; an unsafe-url value in a response header is covered by DPK-DAST-068 instead.
recordDesc: unsafe-url in a meta referrer element sends the full page URL, path and query to every destination, including plaintext origins. Tokens, invitation keys and user identifiers commonly sit in the query string, so a single outbound link or image can move them to a third party log.
applicability: Responses whose page content sets a referrer policy through a meta element.
risk: Sensitive query parameters are disclosed to third parties and to plaintext destinations through the Referer header of every outbound request.
why: A meta referrer element sets unsafe-url.
fix: Remove the meta element and set Referrer-Policy as a response header.
Keep tokens out of query strings where the page can avoid it.
verifyT: Click an outbound link and confirm the Referer header carries the origin only.
